title: The Truman Show
wiki_lead:
The Truman Show is a 1998 American comedy-drama film directed by Peter Weir, and written and co-produced by Andrew Niccol. It stars Jim Carrey as Truman Burbank, a man who is unaware that he is living on a colossal soundstage, and that his life is the subject of a reality television show. The supporting cast includes Laura Linney, Ed Harris, Noah Emmerich, Natascha McElhone, Holland Taylor, and Paul Giamatti.
Niccol's original spec script was more of a science-fiction thriller, with the story set in New York City. Producer Scott Rudin purchased the script and set up production at Paramount Pictures. Brian De Palma was to direct before Weir signed on as director, making the film for $60 million—$20 million less than the original estimate. Niccol rewrote the script while the crew was waiting for Carrey to sign. The majority of filming took place at Seaside, Florida, a master-planned community located in the Florida Panhandle.
The Truman Show held its world premiere in Los Angeles on June 1, 1998, and was released in North America on June 5. It was a financial success, grossing $264 million worldwide, receiving critical acclaim, and earned numerous nominations at the 71st Academy Awards, 56th Golden Globe Awards, 52nd British Academy Film Awards, and 25th Saturn Awards. The Truman Show has been analyzed as an exploration of simulated reality, existentialism, surveillance, metaphilosophy, privacy, and reality television, and as a genre-blending work that features elements of romantic comedy, psychological drama, science fiction, metafiction and social satire. The Library of Congress selected it for preservation in the National Film Registry in 2025 as "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant".

Plot
Selected at birth and legally adopted by a television studio following an unwanted pregnancy, Truman Burbank is the unsuspecting star of The Truman Show, a reality television program filmed and broadcast worldwide, 24/7, through hidden cameras. Truman's hometown, Seahaven Island, is set inside an enormous soundstage in Los Angeles, which allows Christof, the show's creator and executive producer, to control nearly all aspects of Truman's life. Truman's world is populated by actors and crew members who serve as his community while keeping him from discovering the truth. To prevent Truman from escaping, Christof has orchestrated various scenarios such as the "death" of Truman's father in a boating accident to instill thalassophobia, and has the cast reinforce Truman's anxieties with messages about the dangers of traveling and the virtues of staying home.
Though the producers intend for Truman to fall in love with and marry a woman named Meryl, he develops feelings for an extra named Sylvia. Sympathetic to Truman's plight, Sylvia tries to tell him the truth, but is promptly fired and removed from the set. grok_lead: The Truman Show is a 1998 American psychological comedy-drama film directed by Peter Weir and written by Andrew Niccol, starring Jim Carrey in the title role as Truman Burbank, an insurance salesman whose idyllic life in the coastal town of Seahaven is revealed to be an elaborate, 24-hour-a-day reality television program broadcast worldwide without his knowledge, orchestrated by producer Christof ( Ed Harris) from a massive studio simulating an entire world. The film features supporting performances by Laura Linney as Truman's wife Meryl, Noah Emmerich as his best friend Marlon, and Natascha McElhone as Sylvia, a former actress who attempts to alert Truman to the deception. Produced by Paramount Pictures with a budget of approximately $60 million, it earned over $264 million worldwide at the box office, marking a commercial success that contrasted with Carrey's prior comedic roles by showcasing his dramatic range. Critically acclaimed upon release, The Truman Show received a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and garnered three Academy Award nominations for Best Director, Best Supporting Actor, and Best Original Screenplay, along with a Golden Globe win for Harris in a supporting role. Its prescient exploration of media manipulation, surveillance, and the commodification of personal authenticity anticipated the rise of reality television and digital voyeurism, influencing cultural discourse on privacy and simulated realities in the ensuing decades.
